threads.thread_goal: Align on current loading, stacking and cleaning practices and main pain points.

messages.text: Kickoff for Warehouse Loading Bay Safety and Efficiency Upgrade. For T1 we need to map how we actually load, stack and clean today so A5 later makes sense. Can each of you describe how a typical truck is handled now: steps from arrival to departure, how you stack pallets or containers, and what cleaning or quick inspections you do around the dock between trucks

For mixed pallet loads now: truck backs in, we check seal and paperwork, then I usually start with the heaviest pallets at the front of the trailer and work back. I try to follow the drop order but under time pressure we sometimes just fill the space. Stacking wise, we go up to 4 layers on standard pallets, sometimes 5 if the wrap looks strong. Cleaning is mostly sweeping when we see a lot of shrink wrap or broken wood, not on a fixed routine.

On my shift for full truck loads we do a quick visual check of the trailer floor and the dock plate, then load by zones: heavy pallets first over the axles, then lighter ones. For stacking, we usually respect the pallet label but there is no written rule on max layers. For dangerous goods we rely on the pictograms but I see different interpretations, especially on mixing them with normal pallets. Cleaning is end of shift: quick sweep, pick up broken boards, check that exits are not blocked.

From my side on the floor: when a truck leaves, if there is time I sweep the ramp and around the dock, and pick up plastic and straps. If it is busy, I only clear what is directly in the way of the next truck. I do not have a checklist, I just look at the obvious spots like in front of the doors and near the forklift parking.

I usually help with unloading raw materials. We lower the dock plate, check that the pallets are not leaning, then I bring them out with the forklift. I put damaged pallets aside but there is no fixed place for them. For cleaning, I mostly do it when someone points out a spill or loose wrap. We do not record anything, it is just done on the spot.

Thanks, this matches what I see. For T1 we also need to capture unsafe shortcuts. Examples I notice: loading heavy pallets at the back when we are rushing, stacking higher than the pallet label, and skipping trailer floor checks when the driver is pushing. Can you confirm if this happens on your runs too, especially on the main city route and the regional mixed route

Yes, on the main city route we sometimes put lighter pallets first just because they are staged closer, then squeeze the heavy ones at the back. Also, when we are late, I have skipped checking the trailer floor for nails or holes. For stacking, I have gone one layer above what feels safe when the truck is almost full.

On the regional mixed route, the main shortcut is loading by what arrives first at the dock, not by drop order. That means we sometimes have to move pallets inside the truck at the customer. For dangerous goods, I have seen them placed near the doors for quick access, but not always with separation from food or fragile goods.

On cleaning: sounds like we are all doing it reactively. For the new checklist later (A3) and the tracking sheet (A8) we will need to define fixed times per shift. For now, can you both list the top three spots where you most often see debris or spills so we capture them in T1 as pain points

The worst spots I see: right at the dock edge where wrap and straps fall, around the forklift parking where oil drips sometimes, and near the emergency exit by dock 3 where people leave broken pallets.

I agree with those and would add the ramp between the warehouse and the loading bay. When it rains, water and mud get dragged in and it gets slippery. Also the corner near the waste container where we stack damaged pallets is often messy.

For T1 I can start a simple list of current steps for three cases: full truck load outbound, mixed pallets outbound, and inbound raw materials. I will note where we lose time and where we cut corners, then share it here for everyone to check before we move on to drafting A1.

That helps. One more point: we need to decide which load types and routes we focus on first for the new procedures so T1 and later A5 are not too broad. My suggestion is: 1) outbound full truck loads on the main city route, 2) outbound mixed pallets on the regional route, and 3) inbound raw materials on dock 2. These cover most of our volume and the main issues we mentioned.
I am ok with those three. They are where we feel the most pressure and where the stacking and sequence problems show up the most.
Works for me too. I spend most of my time on inbound raw materials and see many of the same issues repeating there.
Agreed on those three focus areas. Once I finish the step mapping for T1 I will structure it by those cases so we can plug it straight into the draft SOP A1 and later into the pilot log A5.

To close this thread: we will focus on outbound full truck loads on the main city route, outbound mixed pallets on the regional route, and inbound raw materials on dock 2. Next step is to complete T1 with current steps, bottlenecks and shortcuts for those three, then we move to drafting A1 and the stacking rules A2.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the draft SOP and stacking guideline before pilot.

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the loading and unloading SOP A1 and the stacking and weight rules A2 based on T2 and T3, plus a section on special loads from T12 that will later feed into A6. Can you all review the structure and call out anything that is unclear or missing before we lock it for the pilot

On A1, the pre-checks section is clear: trailer floor, dock plate, forklift check. For loading sequence, you wrote: load by drop order, heaviest pallets over the axles, then lighter ones. That matches how we want to work. One thing I am not sure about is the part on when to refuse a trailer if the floor is damaged. Maybe we need a simple rule or example there.

I went through A2. The table with max layers per pallet type is helpful. For standard pallets you set 4 layers max, 3 for mixed fragile loads, and 2 for dangerous goods. That feels safe. For mixed loads, the examples are good but I suggest we add one case where we have both food and chemicals, since that happens on the regional route.

I read the unloading part of A1. The steps are easy to follow, but I got a bit lost on the crane notes since I do not use it often. Maybe we can add a short note that those steps are only for people trained on the crane and that others should wait for them instead of trying it.

On the special loads part from T12 and A6, I saw the section about animals and dangerous goods. The animal part is clear for me: calm loading, no shouting, check ventilation. For dangerous goods, I am not fully sure how to read all the pictograms. Maybe we can add a small legend or a picture example in A6 so it is easier on the floor.

Good point on refusing trailers. I propose we add a simple rule in A1: if you see holes, broken boards or soft spots bigger than your hand in the main travel path, stop loading and call the supervisor. For smaller defects, we can mark and avoid them with the forklift. I will write it in plain language so it is easy to apply.

On A2 mixed loads with food and chemicals: we can add an example where chemical pallets are loaded at the back, separated by at least one pallet space from food, and never above them. I will also reference the dangerous goods pictograms from A6 so people can quickly see which pallets count as chemicals.
That example would help. Maybe also add a note that if we cannot keep that separation because of space, we call the planner to adjust the load instead of improvising.

For T2, the post-checks in A1 mention checking that the bay is clear and the dock plate is up before the truck leaves. Could we also add a quick look at the floor for spills or debris so it links with the cleaning checklist later

Yes, I will add a line in A1 post-checks: quick sweep or pick-up of visible debris before the next truck, and a note to tick the cleaning item on A3 once we roll that out. That keeps loading and cleaning connected.

On the crane part, I like the idea of saying only trained people use it. Maybe we can also mark in A1 that if the crane is needed and no trained person is around, we wait instead of trying to improvise with the forklift.

For A6 and T12, I will add a small table with the most common dangerous goods pictograms we see here, a short description, and a simple do and do not for each. That should make it easier to recognise them quickly during loading.
From my side, with these changes, I can follow A1 from start to finish without guessing. The steps match what we do, just more structured. I am ok to use this version in the pilot.
Same for A2. The limits are clear and the examples cover the tricky cases I see. I am fine applying these stacking and weight rules during the pilot.
I am comfortable with the unloading and safety parts in A1 now that we will add the notes on crane use. I can follow it on my shift.
With the pictogram table in A6, I think I will understand the dangerous goods part better. I am ok to follow those rules in the pilot.

Summing up this thread: we will update A1 with the trailer refusal rule, clearer crane notes, and the link to cleaning checks, and A2 with the mixed food and chemical example and the call to the planner if separation is not possible. A6 will get the pictogram table from T12. With these edits, we agree to use A1 as the SOP and A2 as the stacking rules for the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Define cleaning and inspection routines and how they will be tracked.

messages.text: I drafted a new daily cleaning and inspection checklist A3 and a simple tracking sheet A8 for T4 and T11. The checklist covers floors, ramps, equipment and emergency exits, split by shift with estimated time. The tracker has columns for date, shift, completed items and issues. Can you check if the items and timing look realistic for your shifts

I saw A3. For early shift, you put 10 minutes for sweeping the ramps and dock edges. Some mornings it takes me longer when there is a lot of wrap and broken wood. Maybe we should allow a bit more time or say that heavy clean-up can be split with someone else.

On A3, I like that there is a specific line for checking that emergency exits are clear. For the mid shift, you put a quick walk to check for spills and loose wrap. That is fine, but maybe we should add the forklift parking area as a named spot so we do not forget oil drips.

For A8, the tracker is simple enough. I suggest we add a short field for near-misses, like almost slipping or almost hitting debris with the forklift, not only actual incidents. That will help when we review A5 after the pilot.

On T4, the checklist items look complete: floors, ramps, equipment, exits. I would just make sure we clearly say who does what per shift so it does not get skipped when we are busy. Maybe add a column for role, like mover or factory hand, next to each item in A3.

Good point on time. We can increase the early shift ramp and dock edge cleaning from 10 to 15 minutes in A3, and add a note that if there is an unusual amount of debris, the mover on that dock helps for a few minutes.
I will add forklift parking as a named spot in the mid shift walk in A3, and also in the tracker A8 as a common issue location so we can see patterns.
I like the near-miss idea. I will add a small column in A8 called near-miss so we can log those quickly, and later we can copy the main ones into A5 when we review the pilot.
Having a role column in A3 would help me know which parts I am responsible for. Sometimes I am not sure if I should clean around the dock plate or if the mover does it.
I will add that role column in A3 and fill it with who usually does it now: for example, factory hand for ramps and exits, mover for quick sweep around the dock plate between trucks.
On T11 and A8, where will we keep the tracker so everyone can see it and update it Do we plan to print it and keep it on a clipboard, or use a board on the wall

My suggestion: we print A3 as checklists on clipboards for each dock, and we use A8 as a weekly sheet on a whiteboard near the time clock. After each shift, the person responsible ticks completed items on A3 and then copies the result and any issues into A8 before leaving.
I can handle filling A8 at the end of my shift if it is on the whiteboard. That is easier for me than going to a computer.
Whiteboard near the time clock works for me too. It is visible and we can quickly see if a shift missed something.
With the time adjustment and the added spots, A3 looks doable on my shift. I am ok to use this checklist as our standard content.
I agree. A3 now covers the key areas we listed in TH1 and fits into the shift without being too heavy. I support using this version as the standard checklist.

So we go with printed A3 on clipboards at each dock and A8 as a weekly sheet on the whiteboard near the time clock. End of each shift, the assigned person updates A8 with completion and issues. I will adjust T11 to reflect this setup.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and coordinate the one-week pilot on a selected dock.

messages.text: We need to plan the one-week pilot for T7 using the new SOP A1, stacking rules A2, cleaning checklist A3 and tracker A8, and log issues in A5. Proposal: run the pilot on dock 2, all three shifts, starting next Monday. Dock 2 handles the three focus cases we picked and is close to the supervisor office. Thoughts

Dock 2 makes sense because of inbound raw materials and mixed pallets. All shifts is good to see how it works at night too. We just need to check with the supervisor that there is no planned maintenance there next week.

I am on the early shift at dock 2 most days, so I can help make sure A1 and A2 are followed. Starting Monday works for me. For T5, we should also have the improved loading sequence for the main routes ready so we can test it during the pilot.
I can handle A3 and A8 on dock 2 for late shift. Starting Monday is ok. I will just need a quick run-through of the new forms before we start.
I am fine with dock 2 as well. For night shift, sometimes we are short on people. If that happens during the pilot, should we still try to do all A3 items or focus on the most critical ones

If we are short-staffed at night during the pilot, I suggest we prioritise A3 items that affect immediate safety: spills, debris on ramps and dock edges, and clear emergency exits. Less critical items like deep cleaning corners can move to the next shift. We will note any skipped items in A8 so we see the impact.

On T5, I can finalise the improved loading sequence in A4 for the main city route and the regional route by Friday. Then we can brief the drivers and movers on dock 2 before Monday so they know the new order.
If you share A4 by Friday, I can walk through it with the early shift team and check if the sequence is practical with how goods are staged now.
I will check with the supervisor today about any maintenance or special loads on dock 2 next week. If there is a conflict, we might switch to dock 3, but dock 2 is our first choice.
Before Monday, I can do a short walk-through with you on how to tick A3 and fill A8, so we are aligned on what counts as an issue or near-miss for A5.
That would help, thanks. Once I see it once, I can repeat it each night.

For logging issues during the pilot, I suggest we use A5 as the main log. Each shift writes down any problems with A1, A2, A3 or A4, plus any incidents or near-misses. We can keep a printed copy of A5 on dock 2 and then transfer it to a digital version later if needed.
I like using A5 as a single place for pilot notes. Maybe we can add a simple code in A5 to show which document the issue is about, like SOP, stacking, cleaning or sequence.
Agreed. We will use A5 as the central pilot log on dock 2, with a small code for which part the issue relates to. That will make it easier to adjust documents after T7.
Once the supervisor confirms, I am ok to say dock 2, all shifts, starting Monday for one full week as our pilot setup.
Same here. Dock 2, all shifts, next week works. That gives us enough volume to really test A1, A2, A3 and A4.

To close: pending supervisor confirmation, we run the pilot for T7 on dock 2, all three shifts, for one week starting Monday. We will use A1, A2, A3, A4 and A8 on that dock, and log all issues and near-misses in A5 with simple codes. If dock 2 is not available, we switch to dock 3 with the same plan.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, adjust documents and lock in training plan.

messages.text: Pilot week on dock 2 is done. I summarised the main findings from A5 and feedback from movers and drivers for T8. Overall, truck turnaround improved slightly and we had fewer near-misses, but there were some complaints about extra steps and confusion on special loads. We now need to adjust A1, A2, A3 and A6 where needed, and confirm the training walk-through A7 and T10 before we roll out wider.

From my side, positives: A1 made it easier to remember pre-checks, and A2 stopped us from over-stacking. Issues: some drivers felt the loading sequence from A4 took longer when their drop order changed last minute. Also, the special loads section in A6 was still a bit long to read during loading.

On cleaning, A3 helped me remember the exits and forklift parking every night. The only problem was that when we were very busy, I could not finish all items and I was not sure how to mark that in A8.

Looking at A5, we had a few near-misses where wrap was left on the ramp even though A3 was ticked as done. That suggests we might need to be more specific in the checklist or in the training script A7.

On the loading sequence A4, one idea is to add a short rule in A1 and A4 for last-minute route changes: if the planner changes drop order after we start loading, we either adjust the sequence only if it does not break weight balance, or we log a note in A5 and keep the safer layout. That way we do not rush and create unstable loads.

For A8, we can add a simple code for partially done checklist: for example, tick completed, and write the item number in the issues column if it was skipped due to time. Then we can see patterns and maybe adjust A3 timing or staffing.

On A6, maybe we can move the detailed explanations of special loads into a back page and keep only a short summary and pictograms on the front. During the pilot I only had time to look at the first part.

Agreed. We can keep a one-page front side on A6 with pictograms, key do and do not, and a simple rule for mixing or not mixing, and move the longer text to the back for training use, not for quick reference.

For A3, we could split the ramp cleaning item into two lines: one for big debris like broken wood and one for small wrap and straps. In A7 we can then stress that both need to be checked, not just the obvious pieces.
If we add that code in A8, I can mark which items I had to skip. That will make me feel more comfortable when I cannot finish everything.

On T10 and A7, I drafted a 15-minute walk-through script that covers: 1) quick intro on why we changed things, 2) key steps from A1 and A2, 3) cleaning expectations from A3, and 4) how to log issues in A5 and A8. Each shift lead can use it at the start of the week and for new people.
I like the structure of A7. Maybe we can add one or two real examples from the pilot in A5, like the wrap on the ramp near-miss, to make it more concrete during the walk-through.

For T9, I will update A1 with the last-minute route change rule, A2 only needs a small clarification on mixed loads, A3 will get the split ramp item and clearer wording, and A6 will be shortened on the front page. I will also bump version numbers and add change notes so we know this is the post-pilot set.
Once you update those, I can reprint A3 and A6 and refresh A8 on the whiteboard. That way we start next week already with the final versions.
For the training A7, it would help me if there is a small checklist at the end for the shift lead, so they can tick that they covered each topic. Then we know everyone heard the same message.
Good idea. I will add a short list at the end of A7 with the four main points and a space for date and shift so we can track which teams had the walk-through.
Once the documents are updated, I am comfortable using A1, A2, A3 and A6 as our standard, not just on dock 2. The pilot showed they work if we follow them.
I agree. With the tweaks we discussed, I am ok to treat these as the final versions and roll them out to other docks, using A7 for each shift.

To wrap up: we will finalise A1, A2, A3 and A6 with the pilot adjustments from T9, and use A7 and T10 to run a 15-minute walk-through on each shift next week. With that, we treat these as our standard procedures and cleaning routines going forward.
